steps.action:
Here are three of the main factors that led to the outbreak of World War I:

1. Militarism  
   • In the decades before 1914, the great powers of Europe engaged in an intense arms race.  
   • Rapid increases in defense spending, the build-up of large standing armies, and the glorification of military power created an atmosphere in which leaders and publics alike saw war as both likely and—at least for their side—potentially advantageous.

2. Alliance Systems  
   • Europe had divided into two major alliance blocs: the Triple Alliance (Germany, Austria-Hungary, Italy) and the Triple Entente (France, Russia, Britain).  
   • These alliances were meant to deter conflict, but they also meant that a dispute involving one power could quickly draw in others, turning a regional crisis into a continent-wide war.

3. Nationalism and Imperial Rivalries  
   • Strong nationalist movements—particularly in the Balkans—fueled tensions (e.g., Slavic nationalism challenging Austro-Hungarian authority).  
   • Competing imperial ambitions in Africa, Asia, and elsewhere heightened distrust among the powers and contributed to a willingness to resort to force to defend or expand empires.

(An immediate spark—the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in June 1914—triggered the war, but these deeper causes made a large-scale conflict increasingly likely.)
